'''John Kenneth Stille''' (May 8, 1930 – July 19, 1989) was an American chemist who discovered the [[Stille reaction]]. He received B.A. and M.A. degrees from the [[University of Arizona]] before serving in the Navy during the [[Korean War]]. He received his Ph.D. from the [[University of Illinois]], where he studied under [[Carl Shipp Marvel]].<ref name=Macro>{{cite journal | journal = Macromolecules | title = In memory of John Kenneth Stille | last = Lenz | first = R. W. | year = 1990 | volume = 23 | issue = 9 | pages = 2417–2418 | doi = 10.1021/ma00211a001| bibcode = 1990MaMol..23.2417L }}</ref> Stille began his independent career at the University of Iowa in 1957 before moving to [[Colorado State University]] in 1977.<ref name=organometallics>{{cite journal | title = John K. Stille | journal = Organometallics | volume = 9 | issue = 12 | pages = 3007–3008 | year = 1990 | doi = 10.1021/om00162a001 | last = Hegedus | first = L. S.}}</ref>

While at the University of Arizona, Stille met his wife-to-be, Dolores Engelking.<ref name=Macro/> He and Dolores were married in 1958 and had two sons, John Robert and James Kenneth.<ref name=organometallics/>

Stille was killed at age 59 in the [[United Airlines Flight 232]] crash at [[Sioux City, Iowa]].<ref name=Macro/>

In 2010, the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] was awarded to [[Richard F. Heck]], [[Ei-ichi Negishi]] and [[Akira Suzuki (chemist)|Akira Suzuki]] for their work on [[Palladium-catalyzed coupling reactions|palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/2010/|title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2010|website=www.nobelprize.org|accessdate=February 4, 2018}}</ref> The Stille reaction is a key part of palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling chemistry, and it is thought that Stille was a likely candidate for the Nobel Prize before his untimely death.<ref name=TodayCSU>{{cite web|url=https://source.colostate.edu/|title=Home|website=SOURCE|accessdate=February 4, 2018}}</ref>
